prompt.context: BCG has been hired by an institutional asset manager client. The client is very profitable and doing well. However, they know that they are leaving money on the table: they know that they have a lower average percent fee of assets under management than their competition—lower than the industry average. They've hired BCG to tell them why that is.
prompt.question: Why does the client have a lower average percent fee on assets under management than the industry average? What would you recommend to fix the problem?

clarifying_info.q: How does the client generate revenue?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues are based on fees from clients. Clients are charged a fee structured as some percentage of assets under management.

Large institutional investors such as pension funds (e.g., TIA-CREF, CalPers), foundations, hospitals, and universities. This case focuses on the institutional investor side of the business, not individual 401Ks or mutual funds.

clarifying_info.q: How does the fee percentage vary with client size?
clarifying_info.a: Larger clients—those with more assets under management—are charged a lower percentage fee. The fee structure is a stepped function: as assets under management increase, the percentage fee decreases.
Yes, the client is very profitable and doing well overall.

exhibits.title: Revenue Structure for Institutional Asset Management
exhibits.shows: A stepped-function chart with Fee on Assets Under Management (%) on the y-axis and $ Under Management on the x-axis. The fee percentage decreases in steps as assets under management increase.

exhibits.title: Discounts by Deal
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot with % Discount on the y-axis (ranging from 10 to 100) and $ Under Management in millions on the x-axis (ranging from 10 to 10,000 on a log scale). Each point represents a deal and the discount applied.

data.observation: Highest discounts appear clustered around mid-sized clients rather than the largest clients

framework: Understand the business model: fee structure as % of AUM, stepped downward for larger clients
Analyze cost structure: cost to service a client is roughly the same regardless of client size
Identify the revenue/profitability implication: large clients are highly profitable (more AUM x lower %, same cost)
Examine discount patterns by deal (Exhibit 2): who is getting the largest discounts and why
Diagnose root cause of the low average fee: discounting behavior, especially on mid-sized clients
Recommend fixes: cap discounts, realign discount policy to reward large clients, monitor and track discounting, consider incentive structures for salespeople

questions.prompt: Given the stepped fee structure (Exhibit 1) and that it costs roughly the same to service any client regardless of size, what is the profitability implication for large vs. small clients?
questions.guidance: Large clients are highly profitable: they generate substantial absolute revenue (large AUM × even a small %) while incurring essentially the same servicing cost as a small client. This makes retaining and growing large clients especially valuable. The interviewer expects the candidate to articulate this margin dynamic clearly.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2 (Discounts by Deal), what does the data tell you about the client's discounting behavior, and how does this explain the lower average fee?
questions.guidance: The scatter plot reveals that the largest discounts (up to 90%) are being given to mid-sized clients, not the largest ones. This is counter-intuitive and counter to good pricing strategy. Discounting heavily on mid-sized clients compresses margins on that segment and drags down the overall average fee percentage below the industry average. The candidate should note: (1) biggest discounts are going to wrong segment, (2) no apparent cap on discount depth, (3) discounting appears random/clustered—possibly salesperson-driven.

questions.prompt: If you were the client, what would you want to see in the discount data instead? What is the ideal discount policy?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers at least two or three of: (1) Largest discounts should go to the largest clients (highest AUM), not mid-sized ones, because large clients are the most profitable and worth winning/retaining. (2) There should be a cap on discount depth—discounting up to 90% likely destroys all profit margin; a cap around 30% is a reasonable benchmark. (3) The apparent randomness/clustering suggests discounting is salesperson-driven rather than policy-driven; this needs to be investigated and controlled. (4) A structured tiered discount policy tied to AUM brackets would be more rational than ad hoc negotiation.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key steps the client needs to take to fix the discounting problem and bring their average fee up to at least the industry average?

categories.name: Diagnose root cause
ideas: Identify who gave each discount—map discounts to individual salespeople or account executives
Determine whether discount clusters correspond to a specific salesperson, region, or client type
Understand the business justification (if any) behind each large discount

categories.name: Policy redesign
ideas: Establish a formal discount policy tied to AUM tiers (larger AUM = eligible for larger discount, up to a cap)
Set a maximum discount cap (e.g., 30%) to protect minimum margin
Require management approval for discounts above a threshold

categories.name: Monitoring and tracking
ideas: Implement a system to track all discounts given in real time
Create a dashboard for management to monitor average fee vs. industry benchmark
Regular reporting on discount utilization by salesperson and client segment

categories.name: Incentive realignment
ideas: Redesign sales compensation so that giving large discounts reduces the salesperson's commission
Create incentives for salespeople to win or retain large clients at full or near-full fee
Consider clawback provisions if a deal discounted heavily churns quickly

recommendation: The client's lower-than-average fee is driven by excessive and poorly targeted discounting: mid-sized clients are receiving the deepest discounts (up to 90%) while large clients—the most profitable segment—are not being treated with commensurate priority.

BCG should recommend a three-part fix: (1) redesign the discount policy to cap maximum discounts and tie permissible discount depth to AUM size, (2) implement monitoring and tracking systems for all discounts, and (3) realign salesperson incentives to discourage unnecessary discounting.
risks: Mid-sized clients who have grown accustomed to heavy discounts may churn if discounts are reduced suddenly; a phased rollout with relationship management is needed.
Salespeople may resist or circumvent new policies without strong management enforcement and cultural buy-in.
Capping discounts may cause the client to lose some deals to competitors who are willing to discount more aggressively.
next_steps: Conduct a detailed audit of all existing deals, mapping discounts to salespeople and client types to identify the largest offenders.
Design a new tiered discount policy with a hard cap and present it to sales leadership for feedback before rollout.
Build or procure a discount-tracking dashboard and integrate it into the sales management process.
Redesign sales compensation to incorporate average fee attained as a key performance metric.
